content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors train a code-generating language model for the code refinement task
to make it capable of changing the hyperparameters of neural networks in their
source code. This model is used to generate several candidate improvements to
the model itself by randomly changing its hyperparameters, and a simple genetic
algorithm is used to select the best performing candidate model based on its
loss on training for one epoch. The best model then replaces the current model
and the process starts anew. The authors refer to this process as
"self-programming Artificial Intelligence". There is another variaton where the
code refinement model itself is not replaced, but used to determine the
hyperparameters of another model, and this other model is replaced by its best
performing candidate each iteration. The authors refer to this as "the AI
programming sub-models to perform auxiliary tasks".
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths

The paper is very well written and interesting.

I think that using code-generating language models to self-improve AI is a good
and interesting idea.

### Weaknesses and Questions

I don't believe that true self-programming is achieved by the paper. In my
opinion, the method performs hyperparameter search using a textual (source code)
representation of the neural network, and the language model manipulates this
representation by changing the hyperparameters, but it does not program. What it
does is very far from what is possible in a programming language, even in a
restricted DSL.

As Fig. 4(b) and Fig. 5 show, the method plateus very quickly. Improvements in
the genetic algorithm could maybe help here, even without making it much more
complex. The language model provides the random mutations, maybe these could be
guided to be better than random. A small population of best candidates could be
maintained. Also, recombination could be useful.

The paper provides no comparisons to existing work, making the results hard to
put into context.

The details of the code refinement task and some hyperparameters are missing.

In Algorithm 1, source can either define a model or a train() function. I don't
understand where the train() function is assigned to source.

I believe that Whitley (2021), from which the genetic algorithm was chosen, was
published in 1994.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity

The paper is very well written.

### Quality

I found the overall quality of the paper high, even though I don't think the
results support the claims.

### Novelty

As far as I know, using code generating language models to self-improve AI is a
novel, interesting idea.

### Reproducibility

Reproducibility is hurt by missing details of the code refinement task and some
missing hyperparameters like the optimizer or learning rate.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I found the paper very well written and the core idea interesting. However, in
my opinion, manipulating the hyperparameters of neural networks in their source
code is very far from a self-programming AI.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper’s title “SELF-PROGRAMMING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE USING CODE-GENERATING LANGUAGE MODELS” is awesome.  Many folks including myself are excited and intrigued by any proposed path to the singularity. The paper proposes a method to randomly permute the architecture description of a neural network to improve the performance on some image recognition benchmarks like CIFAR-10 and EMNIST, using a genetic algorithm.  The method trains a T5 transformer LLM on input/output pairs of programmatically generated randomly permuted neural net model descriptions.  Training the T5 LLM on this results in an LLM that will take as input a neural network model description and produce as output a randomly permuted version of that neural network description.  Genetic algorithm is applied to take the best performing new models and iterate.  Note applying this T5 LLM that randomly permutes model descriptions to it’s own model description enables self-modification.  When the method is applied to image recognition models for CIFAR-10 and EMNIST, improvements in accuracy are made.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The main strength is the ambitious goal of a self-programming AI.

A weakness is the T5 LLM isn’t being taught to generate better neural networks, like I would hope to give the T5 LLM a lower scoring model description as input and having a higher scoring model returned as output.  Instead the T5 LLM is just being taught to randomly permute the model description with a programmatically generated trainset.  It’s unclear to me why the method to generate the “Random refinement dataset” used for training the T5 LLM isn’t applied directly to the model descriptions we seek to improve. Does using the T5 LLM  to randomly permute the model parameters work out better or generalize more somehow?  I would have liked a comparison to show using the T5 LLM to randomly permute the model parameters works out better than just applying the simple method to generate the “Random refinement dataset”.  I do greatly respect the topic of this paper and all the hard work that went into it, but I think it would help to read this joke https://joelgrus.com/2016/05/23/fizz-buzz-in-tensorflow/ (gist of it is a complicated expensive machine learning method is used where a simpler piece of code could be used more effectively) and better explain why using an LLM to randomly permute parameters isn’t a tiny bit fizz-buzz-ish.  I might be missing something.  If the T5 LLM was given a low scoring configuration as input and a high scoring configuration as the output during training – and trained to convert low scoring configurations to high scoring – maybe some magic LLM generalization could happen. 

In section 3.1 the loss function seems to be how well the self-programming AI does on learning to generate the random permutations of the random refinement dataset.  That doesn’t make intuitive sense to me of a route to the singularity, even given infinite GPU resources.  It seems like a loss function that better measures how well it solves problems – like would the candidates the T5 generated do better on learning to produce better image recognition networks?  Since the model is just being taught to randomly permute parameters of the model, rather than actually produce better models – the loss function doesn’t seem setup to succeed in producing smarter models.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I love the references to Schmidhuber, he did so much creative and clever work in this field in the 80's, 90's when they had almost no compute to work with (and he continues to do cool stuff), I sometimes think if Schmidhuber had a datacenter of A100 back in 1987 - he and his collaborators would have solved AI long ago.  Unfortunately though for this paper I don't think Shmidhuber left any easy novelty aspects to claim for self-programming AI.  I don't find the implementation described here practical or scaling with infinite compute.

I think I could code up what is described here, I think it is well enough described, although more detail on the size of the random refinement dataset would be nice, and how long it was trained.
content.summary_of_the_review: A "self-programming AI" is a great topic for a paper, but a more compelling implementation is needed, with a loss function that gives some hope that goal could be achieved if infinite compute was added.  I think the implementation describes a genetic algorithm that uses a T5 LLM to randomly permute parameters, but doesn't have a loss function or training regime that could scale up the abilities of models being evolved to do something state of the art.  Folks like Schmidhuber and others have done many creative/clever papers on self-programming approaches and I don't think this paper has added anything compelling.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper tries to optimize a given neural network model in an iterative self-programming approach.
It proposes to first enable the model synthesizing new code snippet on model architecture and training strategy and secondly train a new model with the aforementioned model architecture and training strategy. The paper also claims this approach can programming models for other tasks and provided conducted experiments on CIFAR-10, MNIST, and EMNIST.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The idea of self-programming AI is intriguing but also lack clear defined success criteria. This paper defined a narrowed definition of self-programming AI so that concrete experiments can be conducted and the system can be evaluated.
2. The paper shows that the code generation model can not only modify its own source code for better performance, but can also generalize to program other models in an iterative way.

Weaknesses:
1. The overall definition of self-programming in this paper is too narrow. It is almost only about modify very limited hyper-parameters on the model architecture and learning dynamics. The experiment results are not convincing in that 
    
    - Self modify: no solid gain from the self-modify approach as shown in Figure 1.
    -  Modify sub-model: the experiments are not conducted under any form of constraints (such as find the best neural arch under the same computing budget). So the conclusion is basically generate model arch with larger parameter scale which seems to be a trivial finding.

2. Figure 2,3,4,5 are all lack of title, definition of x and y axis which creates barrier for reader.

3. Figure 2 is the mean results of this paper. But only model 0,1,2,3 and 10 are shown but model 4 to 9 are missing. It is not denoted anywhere the reason for this and thus hard to tell if model 10 are cherry picked. If put aside model 10, then the main contribution of this paper is not clear as no significant loss improvement was found compare to the baseline model 0.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
1. Very little details are provided regarding to "the Random Refinement Dataset". This including missing the description of the dataset size, dataset source, dataset collection procedure, dataset distribution, programming language distribution of the dataset. No quantitive data was provided regarding to data used for "the Random Refinement Dataset".
2. Lack the definition of "learning dynamics" which belongs to the optimizing objective in self-programming in this paper.

2. Novelty:
- Doing neural architecture search in a code generation way is somewhat new.

3. Quality
- The overall quality of this paper is poor, because of the lack of clear definition of the optimizing objective, the lack of information about the dataset, and the lack of baseline (neither on the code generation side or the auto ML side). 

4. Little information around reproducibility is disclosed.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposed a new approach to do neural architecture search and improve its performance, for both self modification and also upgrading sub-models. The idea is novel but the paper lacks concrete description over objective definition, dataset, and baseline. The experiment results support the paper's claim poorly in that little baseline is compared, and the the main observation is Figure 1 is weak with only 1 out of 4 self-programmed model outperformed the original model.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper is a demonstration that it is possible for a code generation model to modify its own training code. It is essentially a neural architecture search work, except that the modifications are made by the code generation itself.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
This paper is an interesting demonstration that a code generation model can modify its own training code.

Weakness:
While it's interesting, my main concern is the lack of technical substance.

This is fundamentally a neural architecture search, and is described clearly in section 4.1 and table 1. The parameters are the usual architecture parameters: number of layers for the encoder, number of layers for the decoder, hidden dimension, number of attention heads, etc. The code generation model can only modify these, -- see table 1. Since the code generation model does not take into consideration of the performance of past trials, its role is just to create random modifications to the architecture parameters. And then samples of these modifications are evaluated by a short training run to select the best one. In summary, I do not see a real difference between the proposed method and a neural architecture search that uses random perturbations, and it seems that just the source of randomness is replaced by the code generation model.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity is good.

Quality is fair.

Novelty is poor.

Reproducibility is good.
content.summary_of_the_review: It's an interesting demonstration of a code-generation model modifying itself, but is fundamentally a neural architecture search with a different source of randomness. There is not enough innovation.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a self-programming language model that can learn to modify it's own code. This model is then used to sample multiple source codes for the model itself and then evaluated on a small subset of training data to choose the best performing model (similar to evolutionary algorithms).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The idea of self-programming AI is very interesting. However, the execution of this idea in this paper is poorly done.

The entire self-programming LM concept in this paper seems unnecessary. Why train the LM on a random refinement dataset and then sample source codes from it when you can just generate random source codes procedurally (which you already do it in the random refinement dataset)?  

It appears that the core idea of this paper just boils down to randomized genetic algorithm. And there is no quantitative comparison to pure genetic algorithm based architecture search, which is an important baseline for this paper.  

Additionally, the improvements in the loss curves in Figures 2 and 3 could just be from the additional model-training rather than from the change in the model architecture.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper has some clear technical flaws (see above)
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper has clear technical flaws and is missing several critical baselines.
